lines: Notice what's actually missing here: not a crash, but an announcement.
The write itself may have gone through fine on both servers. What never happened is the leader telling anyone it succeeded before it went down.
That gap, between doing something and announcing it, is where this entire topic lives.
Before deciding, ask what the rest of the cluster actually knows about this entry.
Most of the servers have never seen it at all. Whatever rule decides commitment has to work from what the majority holds, not from what one server intended.
answer: Not committed, and the new leader is free to overwrite it.
Only two servers out of five ever held this entry, and commitment requires a majority.
Nothing was promised to a client yet, so nothing is being taken back.

lines: Pay attention to what a term is actually doing here, not just what it's called.
It's a number that only ever goes up, and whoever hears a higher one immediately treats their own information as outdated.
A stale term isn't an error to recover from. It's simply rejected on sight.
Watch exactly what the voter is checking, because it's narrower than it sounds.
Not whether the candidate is trustworthy, not whether it's been leader before. Only whether its log is at least as current as the voter's own.
That one check, run by every voter, is the entire reason a newly elected leader can be trusted to already hold every committed entry.
Notice this gets enforced constantly, not verified once and trusted afterward.
Every single append carries a check against the entry right before it. Any mismatch gets refused on the spot, and the leader backs up and repairs from there.
Agreement at one point in two logs isn't a coincidence; it's been forced the whole way back.
Go slowly through this part, because it's the one place intuition tends to point the wrong way.
An entry sitting on a majority looks committed. It isn't, if it came from an earlier term than the leader currently holding power.
Only once the current leader gets one of its own entries onto a majority does the whole earlier history become locked in behind it.
Consider what changing the cluster's membership actually threatens, if done carelessly.
Switch everyone over at once and you can't guarantee it happens everywhere at the same instant. Switch piecemeal without a plan, and two separate majorities might each think they're in charge.
The fix asks for agreement from both the old group and the new group at the same time, for as long as the transition lasts.
Carry forward the shape of the whole argument, not five separate rules.

A clock that rejects the past. A vote that enforces completeness. A log check that forces agreement backward. A commit rule that only trusts the leader's own term. All of it aimed at one goal: every state machine ends up executing identical commands, in identical order.
That goal is the only thing any of these mechanisms were ever for.
Before answering, think about what actually has to be true for a vote to go a certain way.
If an entry is already sitting on a majority, every future candidate has to get a vote from someone in that majority to win at all.
answer: No, it's committed, and no later leader can erase it.
Winning an election requires contacting a majority, and every server in that majority already holds this entry.
Any candidate missing it fails the up-to-date check against every one of them, so it simply can't win.
